title: My Family and My Home
overview: Where you live and who you live with are the next things anyone asks you, and the next things any form wants. This unit gives you four patterns for describing a place and the people in it: saying what you have, saying what belongs to whom, saying what is in a room, and saying exactly where. By the end you can describe your home to someone who has never seen it, and read a rental listing without missing the thing that costs you money.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. It covers all four patterns.
Open Patterns. Work the card, then the worked example, then the practice — in that order.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a rental listing, and the exercise on it is the one that matters most.
Do the Practice. Try each one before you open its answer.
Record yourself describing one room, and play it back.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
In the last unit you learned to say who you are. Now you say where you live and who is with you — the two things people ask about next, and the two things every form wants.
Four patterns, and the first one is a verb you will use constantly.
Have got. This is how English says what you own, what you possess, and often what your home contains. I have got a flat. She has got two children. We have got a small kitchen.
Notice it is two words, and notice the second one never changes. Got is always got. What changes is the first word: have for I, you, we and they — and has for he, she and it. It is the same split you already know from am, is and are. One person or one thing takes has; everything else takes have.
You will also hear people say it without got. I have a flat. She has two children. That is equally correct, and slightly more formal. Both are fine. Use whichever comes out.
For the negative and the question, keep the same shape. I have not got a car. Have you got a key? Has she got children?
Second pattern: the apostrophe s. English shows that something belongs to someone by putting apostrophe s on the owner. My brother's flat. The landlord's number. My daughter's room.
Here is the thing to understand, because it is where the mistake comes from. The apostrophe goes on the OWNER, not on the thing owned. My brother's flat — the apostrophe is on brother, because the brother is the one who owns it. Not brothers flat. Not brother flat's.
And it is not a plural. Two brothers means two people. My brother's flat means one flat belonging to one brother. The apostrophe is the whole difference, and it is silent — you cannot hear it, only see it.
Third pattern: there is and there are. This is how English says that something exists in a place. There is a table in the kitchen. There are two windows in this room.
There is for one thing. There are for more than one. And here is the useful part: the word there does not mean a place here. It is just how English starts this kind of sentence. The actual place comes at the end — in the kitchen, in this room.
Fourth pattern: where exactly. In. On. Under. Behind. Next to. Between. These are prepositions, and they are the words that tell someone where to find something.
English is fussy about in and on. In means inside something — in the cupboard, in the drawer, in the room. On means touching the top surface — on the table, on the floor, on the wall. A book in the table would mean the book is inside the wood.
Between takes two things: between the bed and the window. Next to takes one: next to the door.
These four patterns together let you describe any room to somebody who cannot see it. That is what the last part of this unit asks you to do.
Go to Patterns and work through the four cards.

words.meaning: A home on one floor, inside a larger building.
words.example: I have got a small flat.
practice: The flat is on the third floor.
We are looking for a flat.
words.tutor: Describe a flat in three sentences using have got. You may invent it.

words.meaning: A building where people live, usually with more than one floor.
words.example: There is a house at the end of the street.
words.tutor: Say one sentence about a house and one about a flat, and say what the difference is.

words.meaning: One of the separate spaces inside a home or a building.
words.example: There are four rooms in the flat.
practice: We need a room for the baby.
words.tutor: Count the rooms where you live and say the number in a full sentence.

words.meaning: The room where food is prepared and cooked.
words.example: There is a table in the kitchen.
practice: The kitchen is next to the bathroom.
words.starter: There is a table in the
words.tutor: Say three things that are in a kitchen, each with there is or there are.

words.meaning: The room with a bath or shower and a toilet.
words.example: The bathroom is on the left.
words.tutor: Ask where the bathroom is in three different polite ways.

words.meaning: The room where you sleep.
words.example: The flat has two bedrooms.
practice: My bedroom is at the back.
There is no window in the bedroom.
words.tutor: Say how many bedrooms a home has, using both have got and there are.

words.meaning: The part of a wall you open to go in or out.
words.example: The door is behind you.
practice: There is a door between the two rooms.
words.tutor: Say where a door is using two different prepositions.

words.meaning: The opening in a wall, with glass, that lets in light.
words.example: There are two windows in this room.
practice: The window is next to the door.
There is no window in the kitchen.
The window does not close properly.
words.tutor: Count the windows in the room you are in and say it in a full sentence.

words.meaning: A flat surface on legs, for eating or working at.
words.example: The keys are on the table.
practice: There is a table in the kitchen.
Put it on the table, please.
The table is under the window.
words.tutor: Say where three different things are, all of them using the table.

words.meaning: A seat for one person, with a back.
words.example: There are four chairs.
practice: The chair is next to the table.
words.tutor: Say where a chair is in relation to a table, three different ways.

words.meaning: The furniture you sleep on.
words.example: The bed is under the window.
practice: There is one bed in this room.
My bag is under the bed.
There are two beds in the room.
words.tutor: Describe where a bed is using under, next to and between.

words.meaning: A piece of furniture with doors, for keeping things inside.
words.example: The plates are in the cupboard.
practice: There is a cupboard behind the door.
Put it in the cupboard, please.
There are no cupboards in the kitchen.
words.tutor: Say what is in a cupboard and what is on it. Notice the two prepositions do different jobs.

words.meaning: Your female parent.
words.example: My mother's house is near here.
practice: Her mother has got three children.
words.tutor: Say two sentences about a mother, one with have got and one with the apostrophe s.

words.meaning: Your male parent.
words.example: My father's name is on the form.
practice: His father has got a car.
words.tutor: Use father's twice in two different sentences and check the apostrophe is on father.

words.meaning: Your male child.
words.example: Their son is at school.
practice: My son has got a bicycle.
Her son's room is very small.
My son is nine years old.
words.tutor: Say how many sons someone has, then say something that belongs to one of them.

words.meaning: Your female child.
words.example: My daughter has got her own room.
words.tutor: Say one thing your daughter has and one thing that belongs to her. You may invent her.

words.meaning: A boy or man with the same parents as you.
words.example: My brother's flat is upstairs.
practice: My brother has got a key.
words.tutor: Say I have got two brothers, then My brother's flat. Ask the tutor what the difference in spelling is.

words.meaning: A girl or woman with the same parents as you.
words.example: My sister has got three children.
practice: My sister's room is next to mine.
words.tutor: Say the difference out loud: my sisters, and my sister's. They sound identical — only the writing shows it.

words.meaning: Inside something.
words.example: The plates are in the cupboard.
practice: There is nothing in the drawer.
My keys are in my bag.
words.tutor: Say three things that are in something. Check each one really is inside.

words.meaning: Touching the top or the surface of something.
words.example: The keys are on the table.
practice: There is a picture on the wall.
Put it on the chair, please.
My flat is on the third floor.
The bag is on the floor.
words.tutor: Say one sentence with in and one with on about the same object. Ask the tutor which is which.

words.meaning: Below something, with that thing above it.
words.example: My bag is under the bed.
practice: The box is under the table.
There is nothing under the chair.
He put it under the window.
The keys were under the papers.
words.tutor: Hide something and describe where it is using under. Ask the tutor to repeat where it is.

words.meaning: At the back of something, so that thing is in front.
words.example: There is a cupboard behind the door.
practice: The bathroom is behind the kitchen.
The garden is behind the house.
words.starter: There is a cupboard behind the
words.tutor: Describe one thing that is behind another. Then say the same thing using in front of.

words.meaning: Beside something, with nothing in between.
words.example: The bed is next to the window.
practice: The kitchen is next to the bathroom.
There is a chair next to the door.
My flat is next to theirs.
words.starter: The bed is next to the
words.tutor: Describe a room using next to three times. Ask the tutor to draw it back to you in words.

words.meaning: In the space with one thing on each side.
words.example: The table is between the window and the door.
practice: There is a chair between the two beds.
The bathroom is between the bedrooms.
words.tutor: Between always needs two things. Say a sentence with between and check you named both.

words.meaning: The money you pay each month to live in a place you do not own.
words.example: The rent is due on the first.
practice: The rent has gone up again.
We pay the rent every month.
Is the rent per week or per month?
words.tutor: Ask about rent in three different ways. Ask the tutor which one is most polite.

words.meaning: The person who owns a home and rents it to you.
words.example: The landlord's number is on the form.
practice: The landlord has got the other key.
I have written to the landlord.
The landlord is coming on Tuesday.
words.tutor: Say one thing the landlord has, and one thing that belongs to the landlord.

words.meaning: The small metal thing that opens a lock.
words.example: I have got two keys.
practice: The key is under the mat.
My neighbour has got a key.
There is only one key for the door.
words.tutor: Say where a key is, using three different prepositions.

words.meaning: The flat surface you walk on; also one level of a building.
words.example: The flat is on the second floor.
practice: The bag is on the floor.
There are four floors in the building.
Which floor do you live on?
words.tutor: Floor has two meanings. Use it once for the ground and once for a level of a building.

words.meaning: On a higher floor of a building.
words.example: The bedrooms are upstairs.
practice: The noise is coming from upstairs.
words.tutor: Say what is upstairs and what is downstairs where you live.

readings.title: One Room, Described Twice
readings.passage:
First, badly.
The room is small. There is furniture. My things are there. It is fine.
You now know nothing. You could not draw it, you could not find anything in it, and you would not know whether you wanted to live in it.
Now again, properly.
The room is small — about three metres by four. There is one window, and it is behind the bed. There is a table under the window and two chairs next to it. There is a cupboard behind the door, and my bags are under the bed because there is no space in the cupboard. The floor is wooden and it is very cold in the morning.
Same room. Same size. The second one you can see.
The difference is not long words. Every word in the second version is in this unit. The difference is that the second one says HOW MANY and WHERE, and the first one does not.
When you describe a place, give the number and give the position. There is one window. It is behind the bed. That is the whole skill.

readings.title: What a Rental Advert Does Not Tell You
readings.passage:
An advert for a flat is written to make you come and look at it. It is not written to tell you everything.
So read it twice. The first time for what it says. The second time for what it does not say.
Things adverts often leave out:
Whether the rent includes the bills. If it says rent only or plus bills, you pay more than the number you first saw.
Whether there is a deposit, and how much. This is money you pay before you move in and get back when you leave.
Which floor it is on, and whether there is a lift.
Whether the furniture in the photograph stays. Furnished means it stays. Unfurnished means the room will be empty.
How long the agreement is for.
A useful habit: before you visit, write down the three questions the advert did not answer. Ask them at the door. If the answer to any of them is unclear, that is information too.
One more thing. Words like cosy, compact and bijou usually mean small. Words like in need of some modernisation usually mean old and not repaired. These are not lies. They are choices about which true thing to say.

readings.title: Rental Listing
readings.setting: An advert for a flat, of the kind you would find online or in a window.
readings.passage:
TO LET — 2 BEDROOM FLAT
Park Road, Northfield

Rent:        850 per calendar month
             (plus bills — gas, electricity, water)
Deposit:     980, returned at end of tenancy
Available:   14 April

Floor:       3rd floor — no lift
Rooms:       2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom, kitchen,
             living room
Furnished:   Part furnished (beds and cupboards
             stay; table and chairs do NOT stay)
Heating:     Electric
Parking:     On street only — permit required

Minimum tenancy: 12 months
No pets. No smoking.

Viewings:    Saturdays only, by appointment
Contact:     Northfield Lettings, 0300 774 2210

comprehension.q: In the second description, where is the window?
comprehension.why: The second paragraph says there is one window and it is behind the bed. The first description does not mention a window at all.

comprehension.q: Why are the bags under the bed and not in the cupboard?
comprehension.a: Because there is no space in the cupboard.
comprehension.why: The text gives the reason directly, joined with because. This is the kind of detail the first description leaves out entirely.

comprehension.q: The text says the difference between the two descriptions is not long words. What is it?
comprehension.a: The second one says how many and where; the first one does not.
comprehension.why: The last two lines say exactly this, and note that every word in the better version comes from this unit.

comprehension.q: What does furnished mean, and what does unfurnished mean?
comprehension.a: Furnished means the furniture stays. Unfurnished means the room will be empty.
comprehension.why: Both are defined in the list of things adverts leave out. The difference decides whether you need to buy a bed.

comprehension.a: Money you pay before you move in and get back when you leave.
comprehension.why: The text defines it in one line. It matters because it is money you need up front, on top of the rent.

comprehension.q: The text says cosy and compact usually mean small, but calls them choices rather than lies. What does it mean by that?
comprehension.a: They are true words, but the writer chose the true thing that sounds best instead of the plain one.
comprehension.why: This is an inference. The text says the words are not lies but are choices about which true thing to say — reading an advert means noticing what was chosen.

comprehension.q: How many bedrooms are there, and which floor is the flat on?
comprehension.a: Two bedrooms, on the third floor.
comprehension.why: Both are stated plainly — the bedrooms in the heading and again in Rooms, the floor in its own line.

comprehension.q: The rent is 850. How much money do you need before you move in, and why?
comprehension.a: 1,830 — the first month's rent of 850 plus the deposit of 980.
comprehension.why: Neither number is labelled as what you need up front; you have to add them. This is the question that costs people money when they do not ask it.

comprehension.q: You have a table and four chairs. Do you need to bring them?
comprehension.a: Yes. The listing says the table and chairs do not stay.
comprehension.why: Part furnished is the trap — some things stay and some do not, and the listing says exactly which in brackets.

comprehension.q: You work Monday to Saturday and you have a cat. Name two problems with this flat.
comprehension.a: Viewings are on Saturdays only, when you are working; and the listing says no pets.
comprehension.why: Both are in the listing but in different places — one at the bottom under Viewings, one in the short line above it. Finding both means reading to the end.

grammar.title: Have got: what you have
grammar.explanation: This is how English says what you own, what you possess, and often what a place contains. It is two words, and only the first one changes.
grammar.rule:
I have got        We have got
You have got      They have got
He has got
She has got
It has got

Negative: I have not got a car.
Question: Have you got a key?  Has she got children?

Short forms: I've got, she's got, we haven't got.
Also correct without got: I have a flat. She has two children.
grammar.workedExample:
Make a question from: She has got a key.
1. Find the first word of the verb: has.
2. Move it to the front: Has she…
3. Leave got and everything after it exactly where it was: got a key.
4. Change the full stop to a question mark.
Result: Has she got a key?
Notice got never moves and never changes. Only have or has moves.
grammar.mistake: The usual slip is has for the wrong subject — I has got, they has got. The split is the same one you already know from am, is and are: one person or thing takes has, everything else takes have.
grammar.tip: If it takes is, it takes has.
grammar.practice:
Write have got or has got.
1. I ____ two keys.
2. My sister ____ three children.
3. They ____ a small flat.
4. The kitchen ____ no window.
5. We ____ a new landlord.
Then make numbers 2 and 3 into questions.
grammar.answers:
1. have got  2. has got  3. have got  4. has got  5. have got
Questions: Has your sister got three children?  Have they got a small flat?
Number 4 catches people — the kitchen is one thing, so it takes has, exactly like the kitchen is.

grammar.title: The apostrophe s: whose is it?
grammar.explanation: English shows that something belongs to someone by adding apostrophe s to the owner. The apostrophe is silent — you cannot hear it, only see it — which is why this is a writing problem and not a speaking one.
grammar.rule:
my brother's flat      the landlord's number
my daughter's room     the neighbour's key

The apostrophe goes on the OWNER.

Not a plural:
two brothers   = two people
my brother's   = belonging to one brother

More than one owner: my parents' house (apostrophe after the s).
grammar.workedExample:
Write: the flat belonging to my brother.
1. Find the owner: my brother.
2. Add apostrophe s to the owner, not to the thing: my brother's.
3. Put the thing straight after it: my brother's flat.
Result: my brother's flat.
Check it by asking whose. Whose flat? My brother's. If the answer to whose lands on the word carrying the apostrophe, it is in the right place.
grammar.mistake: Two errors, both common. Putting the apostrophe on the thing owned — my brother flat's. And using an apostrophe for a plural — two brother's, which means nothing. Ask whose before you write it.
grammar.tip: Ask whose. The answer is the word that takes the apostrophe.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite using apostrophe s.
1. the room belonging to my daughter
2. the number belonging to the landlord
3. the keys belonging to my sister
4. the flat belonging to my parents (more than one parent)
Then say which of these is a plural, not a possessive:
5. My brothers live upstairs.
grammar.answers:
1. my daughter's room  2. the landlord's number  3. my sister's keys  4. my parents' flat (apostrophe AFTER the s, because there is more than one owner)
5. My brothers live upstairs — this is a plural. It means more than one brother, and it takes no apostrophe at all.
Number 3 is worth checking: keys is plural, but the owner is one sister, so the apostrophe stays before the s on sister.

grammar.title: There is, there are
grammar.explanation: This is how English says that something exists somewhere. The word there does not mean a place — it is simply how this kind of sentence starts. The real place goes at the end.
grammar.rule:
There is  + one thing
There are + more than one

There is a table in the kitchen.
There are two windows in this room.

Negative: There is no window. / There are no chairs.
Question: Is there a lift?  Are there any cupboards?

Short forms: There's a table. (There are has no short form.)
grammar.workedExample:
Say that a room contains two chairs.
1. Count: two — more than one.
2. More than one takes there are.
3. Add the thing: There are two chairs.
4. Add the place at the end: There are two chairs in the room.
Result: There are two chairs in the room.
Now one chair: There is a chair in the room. Only the first two words changed.
grammar.mistake: Using there is for a plural — there is two windows. Count first, then choose. Also watch the question form: it is Is there a lift, not There is a lift with a question mark.
grammar.tip: Count the thing, then choose the word.
grammar.practice:
Write there is or there are.
1. ____ one bathroom in the flat.
2. ____ four chairs in the kitchen.
3. ____ no windows in this room.
4. ____ a cupboard behind the door.
5. ____ two beds and one table.
Then make number 4 into a question.
grammar.answers:
1. There is  2. There are  3. There are  4. There is  5. There are
Question: Is there a cupboard behind the door?
Number 5 is the one to check: when a list has both a plural and a singular, English follows the FIRST thing — two beds is plural, so there are.

grammar.title: In, on, under, behind, next to, between
grammar.explanation: These words say exactly where something is. They are what turns a useless description into one somebody can act on, and English is fussier about in and on than most languages are.
grammar.rule:
in      = inside it        in the cupboard
on      = touching the top  on the table
under   = below it         under the bed
behind  = at the back of    behind the door
next to = beside it         next to the window
between = one on each side  between the bed and the wall

between needs TWO things.
next to needs one.
grammar.workedExample:
The keys are touching the top surface of the table. Which word?
1. Are they inside the table? No — the table is solid.
2. Are they touching its top surface? Yes.
3. Touching the top surface is on.
Result: The keys are on the table.
If you said in the table, you have said the keys are inside the wood. That is the test: in means genuinely inside something.
grammar.mistake: Confusing in and on is the usual one, because many languages use a single word for both. Ask whether the thing is truly inside. The other common slip is between with only one thing named — between the bed needs a second thing to complete it.
grammar.tip: In means inside. If it is not inside, it is not in.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right word.
1. The plates are ____ the cupboard.
2. The bag is ____ the floor.
3. My shoes are ____ the bed.
4. There is a cupboard ____ the door.
5. The table is ____ the window ____ the door.
6. The chair is ____ the table.
grammar.answers:
1. in  2. on  3. under  4. behind  5. between … and  6. next to
Number 2 is the one people get wrong: you are not inside the floor, you are touching its surface, so it is on the floor.
Number 5 needs both halves — between the window and the door. Between with only one thing named is incomplete.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Have got, all six
speaking.instructions:
Say these six out loud, then again without looking.
I have got two keys.
You have got a bigger room.
He has got a car.
She has got three children.
We have got a new landlord.
They have got no cupboards.
Record all six. Play it back and check the has and have went with the right subject — that is the only thing you are listening for.
speaking.tutor: Say all six to the tutor and ask whether any subject took the wrong form.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Ask and answer
speaking.instructions:
Say both sides of these four exchanges, changing your voice for each.
Have you got a key? — Yes, I have. / No, I have not.
Has she got children? — Yes, she has. Two.
Have they got a lift? — No, they have not.
Has the flat got a garden? — No, but there is a small yard.
Now invent four more of your own. Record the last one.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor four have got questions and answer four back.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Whose is it?
speaking.instructions:
Say each of these out loud. They are all written differently and two of them sound the same.
my brother's flat · my brothers · my sister's room · my sisters · my parents' house
Record them. Play it back — you will hear that my brother's and my brothers are identical.
That is the point: this pattern is invisible in speech and only appears in writing, so it is a writing habit you have to build deliberately.
speaking.tutor: Say my sisters and my sister's to the tutor and ask if it can tell them apart. It cannot — nobody can.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Describe one room
speaking.instructions:
Choose one room where you live, or invent one.
Describe it out loud in six sentences. Every sentence must use there is, there are, or a position word.
Say how many of each thing, and where each thing is.
Record it. Play it back and count: how many times did you say a number, and how many times did you say a position word? If either count is below three, do it again — those two things are the whole exercise.
speaking.tutor: Describe your room to the tutor and ask it to say the room back to you. If it gets anything wrong, your description was not precise enough.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Find it from the description
speaking.instructions:
Put a small object somewhere in the room you are in.
Record yourself describing where it is, in two sentences, without naming the object.
Wait an hour. Play the recording back and follow your own directions.
Did you find it from the description alone, or did you need to remember? If you needed to remember, the description was not good enough — record it again.
If someone is with you, describe it to them instead and watch whether they find it.
speaking.tutor: Describe where something is and ask the tutor to repeat the position back in different words.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Ask about a flat
speaking.instructions:
You are telephoning about the flat in Reading 3. Ask these questions out loud, without writing them first.
How much is the rent? · Are the bills included? · How much is the deposit? · Which floor is it on? · Is there a lift? · Has it got a table and chairs? · When is it available? · Can I see it on a weekday?
Record it. Listen back for two things: did every question have the right form, and did you sound like you were asking rather than reading?
Then record it once more and keep the second one.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be the letting agent and answer your eight questions from the listing.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Describe a room so it can be drawn
writing.prompt:
Write eight sentences describing one room.
Every sentence must contain either there is, there are, or a position word from this unit.
Give a number for every thing you mention.
Then give your description to someone and ask them to draw the room — or leave it for a day, come back, and draw it yourself from the words alone.
writing.model: The room is small. There is one window, and it is behind the bed. There is a table under the window. There are two chairs next to the table. There is a cupboard behind the door. My bags are under the bed. There are no pictures on the walls. The door is between the cupboard and the window.
writing.criteria: Eight sentences; every one uses there is, there are or a position word; every object has a number; the drawing made from it matches the room
writing.support: Do not start writing. Stand in the room and count things first — windows, doors, chairs, tables. Write the numbers down. Then turn each number into a sentence. Counting first is what makes the description usable.
writing.extension: Describe the same room again in four sentences instead of eight, keeping all the information. Deciding what to combine is the harder skill.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Ten apostrophes
writing.prompt:
Write ten short sentences using apostrophe s.
Use a different owner in each one.
Underline the apostrophe s in every sentence.
Then go back and write the owner in brackets after each sentence, to check the apostrophe landed on the right word.
writing.model:
1. My brother's flat is upstairs. (brother)
2. The landlord's number is on the form. (landlord)
3. My daughter's school is close. (daughter)
4. My sister's keys are on the table. (sister)
5. The neighbour's car is outside. (neighbour)
6. My mother's house has a garden. (mother)
7. My father's name is on the agreement. (father)
8. The doctor's room is on the third floor. (doctor)
9. My son's bedroom is very small. (son)
10. My parents' flat is in the next street. (parents — more than one, so the apostrophe goes after the s)
writing.criteria: Ten sentences; ten different owners; the apostrophe s underlined in each; the owner written in brackets and matching the underlined word; at least one plural owner with the apostrophe after the s
writing.support: Write the owner in brackets FIRST, before the sentence. Once the owner is on the page, the apostrophe has an obvious home.
writing.extension: Write four more sentences that contain a plural with no apostrophe — my brothers, two keys — and check you did not add one by habit.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Answer the advert
writing.prompt:
Write a short message to the letting agent in Reading 3.
Say who you are, what you are asking about, and ask the three questions the listing does not answer.
End it politely.
Five to eight sentences. You may invent your details.
writing.model:
Hello. My name is T. Novak. I am writing about the two-bedroom flat in Park Road.
I have three questions. Is there a washing machine in the kitchen? How much is the council tax? Is the parking permit included in the rent, or is it extra?
I work on Saturdays. Is it possible to see the flat on a weekday evening?
Thank you. I look forward to hearing from you.
writing.criteria: Says who you are and which property; asks three questions the listing genuinely does not answer; the questions are correctly formed; ends politely
writing.support: Read the listing again with a pen and mark every line that raises a question you cannot answer from the page. Three of those become your message. The questions are already there — you are finding them, not inventing them.
writing.extension: Add a sentence about the Saturday viewing problem and propose a specific alternative time.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the eight mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence below has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each one out correctly, and write which pattern it came from.
1. My sister have got two children.
2. There is four chairs in the kitchen.
3. My brothers flat is upstairs.
4. The plates are on the cupboard.
5. The table is between the window.
6. Has you got a key?
7. The bag is in the floor.
8. My parent's flat is small. (there are two parents)
writing.model:
1. My sister has got two children. (Pattern 1 — one person takes has)
2. There are four chairs in the kitchen. (Pattern 3 — four is plural)
3. My brother's flat is upstairs. (Pattern 2 — the apostrophe goes on the owner)
4. The plates are in the cupboard. (Pattern 4 — inside, so in)
5. The table is between the window and the door. (Pattern 4 — between needs two things)
6. Have you got a key? (Pattern 1 — you takes have)
7. The bag is on the floor. (Pattern 4 — touching the surface, so on)
8. My parents' flat is small. (Pattern 2 — more than one owner, apostrophe after the s)
writing.criteria: All eight corrected; each labelled with the right pattern number; no new mistakes introduced
writing.support: Label first, correct second. Once you know which of the four patterns it is, that card gives you the fix.
writing.extension: Write four wrong sentences of your own, leave them for a day, then come back and correct them.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Have or has
activities.instructions:
Write have got or has got.
1. I ____ a small flat.
2. My brother ____ two children.
3. The kitchen ____ no window.
4. We ____ a new landlord.
5. They ____ three bedrooms.
6. My daughter ____ her own room.
7. You ____ the wrong key.
8. The building ____ no lift.
9. My parents ____ a house.
10. It ____ a small garden.
activities.answers:
1. have got  2. has got  3. has got  4. have got  5. have got  6. has got  7. have got  8. has got  9. have got  10. has got
The ones worth checking are 3, 8 and 10. A kitchen, a building and an it are each one thing, so they take has — exactly as they would take is.
Eight or more correct means the pattern is working. Below eight, read the Pattern 1 card again before moving on.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Where does the apostrophe go?
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each phrase using apostrophe s.
1. the flat belonging to my brother
2. the number belonging to the landlord
3. the room belonging to my daughter
4. the keys belonging to my sister
5. the house belonging to my parents (two parents)
6. the car belonging to the neighbour
Then decide: apostrophe or no apostrophe?
7. My brother____ live upstairs. (two brothers)
8. My brother____ flat is upstairs. (one brother, his flat)
activities.answers:
1. my brother's flat  2. the landlord's number  3. my daughter's room  4. my sister's keys  5. my parents' house  6. the neighbour's car
7. My brothers live upstairs — no apostrophe. This is a plural: more than one brother.
8. My brother's flat is upstairs — apostrophe before the s. One brother, and the flat belongs to him.
Numbers 7 and 8 are the whole point of this exercise. They sound identical and are written differently, and only the meaning tells you which is which.

activities.title: Practice 3 — There is or there are
activities.instructions:
Write there is or there are.
1. ____ one bathroom in the flat.
2. ____ two windows in the bedroom.
3. ____ no cupboards in the kitchen.
4. ____ a table under the window.
5. ____ four flats on this floor.
6. ____ no lift in the building.
7. ____ three keys for the door.
8. ____ a chair between the two beds.
activities.answers:
1. There is  2. There are  3. There are  4. There is  5. There are  6. There is  7. There are  8. There is
Numbers 3 and 6 are the pair to compare. Cupboards is plural so it takes there are, even though the sentence says there are none. Lift is singular so it takes there is. The word no does not change which one you use — the thing being counted does.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Exactly where
activities.instructions:
Choose in, on, under, behind, next to or between.
1. The plates are ____ the cupboard.
2. The bag is ____ the floor.
3. My shoes are ____ the bed.
4. There is a cupboard ____ the door.
5. The kitchen is ____ the bathroom.
6. The table is ____ the window ____ the door.
7. There is a picture ____ the wall.
8. My keys are ____ my bag.
activities.answers:
1. in  2. on  3. under  4. behind  5. next to  6. between … and  7. on  8. in
The in/on pairs are 1 and 7, and 2 and 8. Ask each time whether the thing is genuinely inside. A wall is solid, so a picture is on it. A bag is hollow, so keys are in it.
Number 6 must have both halves. Between with only one thing named is not finished.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Read the listing
activities.instructions:
Use the listing in Reading 3. Answer without reading the whole thing again — find each answer directly.
1. How much is the rent per month?
2. Are the bills included?
3. How much is the deposit?
4. When is the flat available?
5. Which floor, and is there a lift?
6. Does the table stay?
7. What is the shortest time you can rent it for?
8. When can you see it?
activities.answers:
1. 850 per calendar month  2. No — plus bills, which means gas, electricity and water are extra  3. 980  4. 14 April  5. Third floor, and there is no lift  6. No — the listing says the table and chairs do NOT stay  7. 12 months  8. Saturdays only, by appointment
The skill here is scanning: going straight to the line you need instead of reading from the top. Question 2 is the one that costs money — the rent is not 850, it is 850 plus whatever the bills come to.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Describe and check
activities.instructions:
Write six sentences describing the room you are in now. Use there is, there are and at least three position words.
Put the paper away for a day.
Tomorrow, read only your sentences — do not look at the room — and draw the room from them.
Then compare your drawing with the real room.
activities.answers:
There is no key, because the room is yours. The drawing is the answer.
What to look for when you compare: anything in your drawing that is in the wrong place means a position word was missing or wrong. Anything missing entirely means you did not give it a number. Anything you had to guess at means the sentence was vague.
Most people find two or three problems the first time. Rewrite those sentences with a number and a position word, and the description becomes usable.

quizzes.why: My sister is one person, so it takes has — the same split as is. Are got and is got do not exist.
You takes have, and the question is made by moving have to the front. Got never moves.

quizzes.q: Which is correct for a flat belonging to one brother?
quizzes.why: The apostrophe goes on the owner, before the s, because there is one brother. Apostrophe after the s would mean more than one brother.

quizzes.q: My brothers live upstairs. Why is there no apostrophe?
options: Because it is the start of a sentence
Because upstairs is not a thing you can own
Because it is a plural, not a possessive
quizzes.a: Because it is a plural, not a possessive
quizzes.why: Nothing belongs to anybody in this sentence — it simply says there is more than one brother. A plural takes no apostrophe.

quizzes.q: Complete: ____ four chairs in the kitchen.
quizzes.why: Four chairs is more than one, so it takes there are. It is and they are do not begin this kind of sentence.

options: There are no lift in the building.
There is no lift in the building.
There is no lifts in the building.
quizzes.a: There is no lift in the building.
quizzes.why: Lift is singular, so there is. The word no does not change which form you use — the thing being counted does.

quizzes.q: The plates are inside the cupboard. Which word?
quizzes.why: In means genuinely inside something. On would mean the plates were balanced on top of the cupboard.

quizzes.q: The bag is touching the floor. Which word?
quizzes.why: You are not inside the floor — the bag is touching its surface, so it is on. This is the in/on pair that most often goes wrong.

options: The table is between the window.
The chair is next to the table.
The cupboard is behind the door.
My bag is under the bed.
quizzes.a: The table is between the window.
quizzes.why: Between needs two things, one on each side. Between the window and the door would be complete.

quizzes.q: The listing says rent 850 plus bills. What do you pay each month?
quizzes.why: Plus bills means gas, electricity and water are extra, so the real monthly cost is above 850. 980 is the deposit, which is paid once.

quizzes.q: The listing says part furnished, with beds and cupboards staying. What must you bring?
quizzes.why: The listing says in brackets that the table and chairs do not stay. Part furnished always means some things stay and some do not, and the detail is in the brackets.

quizzes.q: Rent is 850 and the deposit is 980. How much do you need before you move in?
quizzes.why: You pay the first month's rent and the deposit together, so 850 + 980 = 1,830. Neither number is labelled as the up-front total — you have to add them.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example before its practice, every exercise has its answer key, and the Answers section gathers them in one place. Practice 6 and Speaking 5 are both designed so a learner working alone can check their own accuracy by waiting a day and then acting on their own description. If you are running this with a group, that delay can be replaced by a partner.

Not have got, which learners pick up quickly. It is in and on, because a great many languages use one word where English uses two, and the fix is conceptual rather than memorised: ask whether the thing is genuinely inside. Once a learner asks that question automatically, the errors stop. Until then, no amount of drilling helps.

teacherNotes.type: The apostrophe is a writing problem only
teacherNotes.note: Speaking 3 exists to make this explicit: my sisters and my sister's are identical in speech and nobody can hear the difference. Learners who are told the rule but never shown that it is invisible tend to assume they are mispronouncing something. Say it out loud once and the confusion disappears.

Reading 3 and its questions are the most useful ten minutes in the unit. Two of the comprehension questions require arithmetic or inference rather than location — what you need up front, and the Saturday viewing clash — because that is what real listings demand and what costs people money when they miss it. Do not let the listing be skimmed.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner, not a marking service, and no task here is scored by it alone. Learners must not be asked to give the tutor personal, immigration, medical or financial details, and should not enter a real address or a real landlord's contact details anywhere in the app. Every task says details may be invented; that wording should not be removed.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what I have and ask what someone else has.
I can write my brother's flat and know why the apostrophe is there.
I can describe what is in a room using there is and there are.
I can say exactly where something is, so someone can find it.
I can read an advert for a flat and find what it does not say.

assignment.title: Describe a home, and read an advert
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, write a description of a home — real or invented — in twelve sentences, using there is, there are and at least five different position words, with a number for every object. Second, find a real rental advert, or use the one in Reading 3, and write down the three questions it does not answer, with the reason each one matters. Keep both together: the first shows you can describe a place, the second shows you can read one.
assignment.submissionType: Written description and a list of questions
